summary.text: A 19-year-old Japanese woman with no prior psychiatric history or psychotropic exposure, with a family history of maternal bipolar disorder, developed elevated mood and grandiose ideas on Day 28 of Month X, then severe anxiety, persecutory ideation, suspiciousness and auditory hallucinations, and was admitted on Day 6 of Month X + 1 for safety.

Evaluation showed hallucinations, delusional ideation and loosening of associations; physical and neurological examinations, head CT, EEG and blood tests including metabolic and thyroid function were normal. She had delusions that food and water were poisoned with refusal of intake, requiring brief physical restraint and intravenous fluids.

Risperidone and olanzapine were started and increased; symptoms improved by the end of Month X + 1, but psychosis acutely recurred on home leave (Day 9 of Month X + 2) and she returned to hospital on Day 11, with gradual restabilization by Day 21.

A cyclical pattern of relapse closely associated with menstruation emerged. A manic episode in Month X + 4 met DSM-5-TR criteria (Bipolar I disorder coding) and responded to aripiprazole with valproate; brexpiprazole was added briefly and discontinued, lithium caused disabling tremor and was stopped with a return to valproate, and relapses continued to align with the menstrual cycle. Risperidone-associated marked hyperprolactinemia (105.4 ng/mL) and antipsychotic-induced amenorrhea occurred, with psychotic relapse even during amenorrhea. The authors give a working diagnosis of menstrual cycle-related psychosis within the bipolar spectrum.

A combined oral contraceptive (drospirenone 3 mg/ethinyl estradiol 0.02 mg, continuous) was started in Month X + 7. Residual flares attenuated, impulse control and premenstrual psychotic features improved by Month X + 8, olanzapine adverse effects (finger tremor, cogwheel rigidity) were reported to have disappeared after its discontinuation in Month X + 9 (Table 1 still lists olanzapine in Month X + 10), and no further relapses were observed by Month X + 10.

She was discharged in Month X + 11 after uneventful trial home leaves and remained stable through Month X + 21 on aripiprazole 24 mg/day, valproate 400 mg/day and the combined oral contraceptive; Table 1 labels Months X + 12 to X + 21 as sustained remission with functional recovery. The authors note no serial hormone measurements and that inferences are hypothesis-generating.

In her own perspective she felt ashamed of behavior during mood highs, found hospitalization, medication changes and side effects burdensome, and reports improved sleep and concentration and relief at feeling stable.
